newsitem.title: UK: UK monetary meeting - key facts.
newsitem.headline: UK monetary meeting - key facts.

text.p: The Bank of England's new monetary policy committee, which has been empowered by the Labour government to set interest rates, held its second monthly meeting this week and will deliver its decision on interest rates at midday on Thursday.
Following are key facts about the meeting:
* The meeting took place at the Bank of England on Wednesday and Thursday morning.
BANK OF ENGLAND -- Governor Eddie George, deputy governor Howard Davies, executive directors Mervyn King and Ian Plenderleith.
OUTSIDE MEMBERS -- Charles Goodhart, Professor of Banking and Finance at the London School of Economics; Willem Buiter, Professor of International Macroeconomics at Cambridge University.

* Sir Alan Budd, chief economic adviser to the Treasury, was at this week's meeting as the non-voting Treasury observer. He will take up his voting position on the committee when he retires from the Treasury later this year.
DeAnne Julius, British Airways Plc chief economist and the last outside appointee, will join the committee in September.

* The committee will vote on interest rates at the end of the meeting on Thursday. The decision will be carried on a simple majority with all six members voting. If the vote is tied, the governor will have a second casting vote.
* A formal announcement on the outcome of the meeting will be made at 1100 GMT/1200 BST on Thursday on Bank of England pages, followed by the usual midday money market operations.
* Minutes of the meeting, including details of any vote taken, will be published by the Bank no later than six weeks after the meeting.
* Members of the committee have been asked not to comment publicly on monetary issues in the week of the meeting and the day after.
* British interest rates were raised on June 6 by a quarter point to 6.50 percent.

* This is the last meeting to be attended by Howard Davies who is leaving the Bank of England in August to become head of the Securities and Investments Board. His replacement will be announced by the Treasury soon, possibly this week.
A second deputy governor will be appointed once new legislation creating the post has been passed. This is not expected before the summer recess.
